clinicalPearls: Presents as a smooth, firm, mobile subcutaneous nodule, with the great majority occurring on the scalp.
Unlike epidermoid cysts, pilar cysts lack a central punctum and characteristically shell out cleanly and intact at surgery.
They are frequently multiple and show an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern in many affected families.
The lining shows trichilemmal keratinisation without a granular layer, abruptly producing dense homogeneous keratin, often with calcification.
Overlying hair may be thinned or lost due to pressure, but the lesions themselves are asymptomatic unless inflamed or ruptured.
A proliferating trichilemmal tumour can arise within a long-standing cyst, presenting as a rapidly enlarging exophytic scalp mass.
Complete excision with the intact capsule is curative and technically easier than for epidermoid cysts.
Rarely, malignant proliferating trichilemmal tumours occur and may recur locally or metastasise, warranting histological review of atypical lesions.
reference.pathophysiology: Pilar cysts derive from the outer root sheath of the hair follicle at the level of the isthmus, and the lining epithelium undergoes trichilemmal keratinisation in which cells enlarge and keratinise abruptly without forming a granular layer. The cavity fills with compact, homogeneous keratin that frequently calcifies. A hereditary autosomal dominant tendency underlies the common multiplicity and scalp predilection, and clonal proliferation of the cyst lining can give rise to a proliferating trichilemmal tumour. Malignant change is rare but recognised, characterised by cytological atypia, infiltrative growth and occasionally metastatic potential.
additionalInvestigations: clinical examination noting absence of a punctum
ultrasonography showing a well-defined cystic scalp lesion, sometimes with calcification
histopathology confirming trichilemmal keratinisation without a granular layer
imaging and wide histological sampling if a proliferating trichilemmal tumour is suspected
family history assessment given autosomal dominant inheritance
redFlags: rapid enlargement or exophytic ulcerated growth suggesting a proliferating or malignant trichilemmal tumour
fixation to deeper tissues or irregular infiltrative margins
a solitary firm scalp nodule with atypical features that could represent metastasis
reference.prognosis: Pilar cysts are benign and excision of the intact capsule is curative with a low recurrence rate. Proliferating trichilemmal tumours are usually benign but may recur locally, and the rare malignant variant can metastasise.
pitfalls: Assuming a rapidly growing scalp cyst is simply inflamed and missing a proliferating or malignant trichilemmal tumour.
Confusing a pilar cyst with an epidermoid cyst and expecting a punctum that is absent.
Rupturing the fragile capsule during excision, complicating complete removal.
Failing to submit an atypical or recurrent lesion for histopathology.
